candidates.title: Comparing AI R&D compute caps and deployment lags
candidates.summary: I’m publishing this a bit rougher than usual because it’s very pertinent to Evan Hubinger’s recent shortform , which advocates for blocking internal deployment as a pacing mechanism over compute reallocation (he mostly discusses it in the context of a risk-assessment-based regime, while this post discusses the policies standalone). (see my response to Evan which also summarizes this post.) I compare 2 classes of policies: AI R&D compute cap : A cap on the percentage of compute used for capabilities R&D, as proposed at pacing-ai.com . Deployment lags/freezes: An X-month lag means that you have to use models X months old for AI R&D (or, AIs at most as capable as the AIs you trained X months ago). [1] A freeze means you pick a capability level above which you can’t use models to do AI R&D. I sometimes separate out internal-only lags/freezes from internal+external (“uniform”) ones. If I just say lag, I mean it as shorthand for lag/freeze. Overall, I think compute caps are similarly good or slightly better than deployment lags/freezes (very possible I’ll change my mind in the future). Ignoring political feasibility, I think the best would be to combine both of them in order to get the immediate slowdown of the cap and the long-term + structural benefits of the lag/freeze. [2] I think it’s close enough that if one is significantly more feasible than the other, we should push for the more feasible one. I prefer internal deployment lags to external deployment lags because I think the societal awareness benefits are larger than the verification costs. Factor Cap vs. lag/freeze Reasoning Capability curve shape Compute cap (weak) Let’s consider lag 6 months vs. cap 10% implemented in Mar 2027, which result in similar TED-AI dates. Compute caps slow now->SAR more than lags, while lags slow SAR->TED-AI more. Here's a quick screenshot of an illustrative example comparing the 2 policies: Aggregating uplift-years, varying point of no return (PONR): The higher the capability level of the PONR, the better lags look relative to caps; if it’s ~SAR then caps look slightly better, if it’s ~TED-AI lags look much better. With lags, you delay higher capability milestones more than you do with caps. We’ll look at total uplift-years divided by a racing baseline, with a baseline of SAR in Jul 2027 and TED-AI in Nov. Uplift-years = ∫ (AI R&D uplift of the best model trained) dt from Jan 2027 until the PONR capability level is passed. [3] No China, SAR PONR: Cap ~2.2x, lag ~2x No China, TED-AI PONR: Cap ~1.8x, lag ~3x No China, uncertainty over PONR [4] (35% before SAR, 65% before halfway from SAR to TED-AI, 80% before TED-AI; same PONR for both policies): Cap ~2x, lag ~2.2x With China + TED-AI pause until China catches up, uncertainty over PONR: Both ~2.4x Other considerations in favor of relatively stronger immediate pacing relative to later pacing: China might just not race in the first place, even if the US did. Pacing is more cooperative than racing. Stronger immediate pacing means more serial time to make a deal, or adjust the pacing regime to be better at higher capabilities. AI improvements harm the ability to do international deals even if they aren’t directly dangerous. See here . Going slower now is more robust against others failing to slow down further in the future. Other considerations in favor of relatively weaker immediate pacing relative to later pacing: Going slower now leads to more overhang, meaning faster progress if the regime is lifted. The effect size of this appears to be fairly modest in our modeling; e.g., if both policies are ended right before the lag gets to SAR, the lag takes 2.1 months to go from SAR->TED-AI while the cap takes 1.9 months. [5] Differences in point of no return capability level Deployment lag Not using your best AIs for AI R&D potentially pushes back the point of no return substantially because it makes it harder for AIs to adversarially prevent humans from aligning future AIs. This effect seems potentially quite large if you’re using e.g. current-level AIs or lower for your AI R&D. Some quick modeling using my highly uncertain estimated PONR gap distribution says that this effect might be very important, e.g. changing lag 6 months vs. cap 10% from roughly equal geomean of uplift-years to lag 6 months being ~2.5x higher. Verification ease / robustness Uniform lag > compute cap ~= internal-only lag. Uniform lag > compute cap ~= internal-only lag. See below for more. Societal awareness Against external deployment lag (Pushing in the opposite direction of verification ease/robustness) Enabling safety research Compute cap (weak) In both proposals, there’s the question of handling safety research: In the AI R&D compute cap proposal, can you have a carve-out for using the non-AI-R&D compute for safety R&D? In the deployment lag proposal, can you have a carve-out for using the non-lagged model to conduct safety R&D? Both seem like similarly difficult problems. Let’s consider each situation in turn: If both have a safety carve-out, then an AI R&D compute cap is better than a deployment lag. The situation is similar except that under the AI R&D compute cap, most compute is forced to be spent on either safety or external inference, leading to more compute being spent on safety than in the deployment lag world. If there isn’t a safety carve-out, then it’s unclear, but my best guess is that an AI R&D compute cap is worse than a deployment lag. There’s a tradeoff where there’s probably less compute used for safety in the compute cap world, but a better model. It’s unclear to me how that shakes out, but at least Evan Hubinger has the intuition that it’s better in the deployment lag case because models are differentially worse at safety. Maximum slowdown amount Compute cap A well-enforced compute cap of 0% could result in very nearly a full pause, while banning use of AIs for AI R&D would not. [6] See an example trajectory: Important for: emergencies, international coordination, strong safety-case-based regimes Robustness to different timelines Unsure Caps are better on short timelines and worse on long ones. Verification In terms of ease of verification: Uniform lag > compute cap ~= internal-only lag. Our guess is that with a uniform lag, ~5% verification error can be achieved with significantly less effort / auditing access, though we’ve done less analysis than for the compute cap. [7] We discuss this attack surface here . Attacks against compute caps and internal deployment lags Depending on their implementation, the verification problem for compute caps and internal deployment lags via auditors will need to deal with three overall classes of attacks: Attacks that free up compute. These are attacks that allow the company to use compute in a way that auditors don’t have visibility into. These attacks include getting off-books compute (hidden compute), using compute that is declared to be idle (fake idle) and having spare compute by actually running workloads more efficiently than what is declared or observed (hidden efficiency). Attacks 1-3 in our previous work. Attacks that turn external inference into capabilities benefits. These are attacks that allow external inference to be used as if it were internal inference by just directly having employees use the external API (launder internal inference), collaborating with third parties for R&D or data generation, or training directly on outputs generated via external inference. This only applies to internal-only lags (because uniform lags also restrict external inference). Attacks 4-6 in our previous work. Attacks that consist of exploiting the ‘non-capabilities’ exemption. This only applies to deployment lags that include an exemption for safety research. Attack 7 in our previous work. Additionally, internal deployment lags have to deal with a fourth class of attack: Doing internal deployment via training runs. This would involve having AIs do AI R&D during training runs, e.g., as part of RL rollouts in post-training. Attack 8 in our previous work. In our previous work , we analyzed how the first 3 classes of attacks are all applicable to a compute allocation cap, unless you did a version of the proposal that had no carve-out for ‘non-capabilities R&D’, in which case you could avoid attack 7, or if you didn’t allow serving customers as a category (in which case you could avoid attacks 4-6). In this supplement on internal deployment lags, we identify three possible ways of implementing an internal deployment lag: Uniform Deployment Lag — covered models must be in cold storage, with no internal or external deployment. Internal Deployment Lag — covered models cannot be internally deployed. Internal Deployment Lag with safety carve-out — covered models cannot be internally deployed except for a carved-out application area (e.g., AI safety research). #1 requires defending against attacks 1-3 and 8, #2 against attacks 1-6 and 8 (it avoids attack 7), and #3 against all eight. Verification measures Quantitatively, we are most worried about attacks #5 and #7. This makes a uniform deployment lag highly attractive from a verification perspective. More here In order to sufficiently defend against attacks in general, it seems necessary to adopt a significant fraction of the measures listed below. Read more Measures 1-7 would be the most important as they address attacks 5-7 (assuming an internal deployment lag or a compute cap). [8] These will require an extensive auditing effort with privileged (not just entry-level employee) access and a lot of technical expertise on the auditing teams. Measure 6 in particular will require having multiple different entities submit to audits, so will greatly increase the auditing capacity necessary. Measures 8-15 might become increasingly important to ramp up to as well, but appear less urgent initially. That being said, they generally have long lead times, so effort put into them early might be necessary in order for the verification to keep error sufficiently low for long enough. ^ Unless noted, lags apply at once: AI R&D switches to the older model on the start date, with no grandfathering of models already in use. ^ In the model the delays roughly add: from Mar 2027, cap 10% plus a 6-month lag delays TED-AI by 23 months, against 11 for each alone. ^ Under a lag this counts the frontier model even though AI R&D can't use it, so it assumes that model still does useful work elsewhere (outside users, wakeup, or a safety carve-out). Counting only the AIs allowed to do AI R&D, the lag scores ~0.7x / ~0.4x / ~0.6x of racing (SAR / TED-AI / uncertain PONR) and the cap is unchanged. ^ Another way to think about this is it’s weighting how much we care about each capability level. From this perspective, one reason to care about higher levels of capability less is that we have more time to intervene before then if the initial policy is suboptimal. ^ The effect is a bit larger if we instead assume they both get lifted at SAR; it takes the lag 2.2 months to get to TED-AI, vs. 1.5 months for the cap. ^ Note that it might be very hard to actually get to ~0%. pacing-ai.com estimates ~6% error even with robust auditing. It might similarly be hard to get to a ~zero error deployment lag/freeze. ^ By 5% verification error, we mean a capabilities gain equivalent to adding a marginal 5% capabilities compute (against the margin of a 20% compute cap). ^ For a uniform deployment lag, these attacks don’t apply, and so these measures aren’t necessary. Discuss

candidates.title: sqlite3_rsync: Database Remote-Copy Tool For SQLite
candidates.summary: sqlite3_rsync: Database Remote-Copy Tool For SQLite This additional SQLite tool has been around for a while now - it was added as "experimental" in SQLite 3.47.0 in October 2024 and enhanced in SQLite 3.50.0 in May 2025 . It was only today that I understood one of its most attractive characteristics. Normally, if you want to grab a snapshot copy of a SQLite database, you need to use either the backup API or VACUUM INTO . In both cases you need enough disk space to create a duplicate copy of your database, so if you're on a small instance and you already use more than half of the available disk you are plain out of luck. sqlite3_rsync can copy a snapshot of your database over an SSH connection to another machine, without first needing to create a full local copy! It's also good for synchronizing an existing copy of a database without re-transmitting the entire thing over the network. It works in a similar way to regular rsync: The core idea behind the protocol is that the replica sends cryptographic hashes for pages or groups of pages over to the origin side. The origin sends back page content that differs, or requests finer-grain hashes if a multi-page hash does not match. If the origin and replica start out being vastly different, the total network bandwidth can exceed the size of the entire database, due to the overhead of exchanging hashes, but the excess bandwidth is not great - a few percent at most. Update : Hah! Turns out I wrote about this application of sqlite_rsync back in October 2024 when the tool was first released. Tags: backups , sqlite

candidates.title: The New York Times warns photographers not to update Photoshop over AI features
candidates.summary: My comment on The New York Times warns photographers not to update Photoshop over AI features — Hacker News. I had a NYT photographer take my picture at my home earlier this year (for a story about Moltbook, oddly enough). At one point I asked if they could fix things up if I had a stain on my shirt and they said absolutely not - they present photographs as they were taken, with cropping and balancing applied but no edits beyond that. He did spend a bunch of time trying to find the best possible natural lighting for the shots he wanted. The photo at the top of https://www.nytimes.com/2026/02/02/technology/moltbook-ai-so... is my laptop, taken in my garden, after hunting around for the best spot that didn't have too much glare on the screen. You can see how dirty my screen is, too! Photography for a newspaper is photo journalism, and they take it seriously. (Thankfully I did not have a visible stain on my shirt.)
